guidance.title: Bowel Obstruction
guidance.summary:
1. **Diagnosing "ileus" without CT to exclude mechanical obstruction.** Post-operative ileus is a diagnosis of exclusion. A transition point on CT distinguishes mechanical SBO (requires surgical evaluation) from ileus (supportive care). CT changes management in 20-30% of cases initially thought to be ileus.

2. **Missing strangulation because labs are normal.** Lactate sensitivity for bowel ischemia is approximately 90% but specificity is low. Normal lactate does not exclude early strangulation. CT findings (reduced wall enhancement, mesenteric edema, pneumatosis) and clinical signs (constant pain, peritonitis, tachycardia) drive the decision.

3. **Delaying NG tube placement.** NG decompression reduces aspiration risk, relieves nausea, and allows quantification of losses for fluid replacement. Place early, not as a last resort.

4. **Under-resuscitating.** Third-space losses in bowel obstruction are massive (3-6 L). Patients presenting with tachycardia and oliguria need aggressive crystalloid before any decision about operative vs. non-operative management.

5. **Failing to examine all hernia orifices.** Incarcerated inguinal, femoral, umbilical, and incisional hernias cause SBO. Missed femoral hernias in elderly women are a classic and preventable diagnostic failure. Examine the groin in every patient with SBO.

6. **Prolonging non-operative management beyond 72 hours for complete SBO.** The risk of strangulation increases with duration. If Gastrografin has not reached the colon by 8 hours, or there is no clinical improvement by 72 hours, surgery is indicated.

guidance.title: Bowel Obstruction
guidance.summary:
- **CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast:** Gold standard. Sensitivity >90% for SBO, identifies transition point, evaluates for strangulation (wall thickening, mesenteric haziness, reduced enhancement, pneumatosis, portal venous gas), closed-loop, and etiology. Oral contrast generally not needed and delays imaging.
- **Abdominal X-ray (upright and supine):** Dilated small bowel loops (>3 cm), air-fluid levels, paucity of distal gas. Sensitivity 60-70% — inferior to CT. Useful for serial monitoring.
- **CBC:** Leukocytosis (strangulation, perforation); hemoconcentration (dehydration)
- **BMP:** Hypokalemia, hypochloremia, metabolic alkalosis (from vomiting and NG suction), elevated BUN/creatinine (prerenal AKI from dehydration)
- **Lactate:** Elevated in bowel ischemia/strangulation (sensitivity 90%, specificity limited)
- **Lipase:** Exclude pancreatitis
- **Urinalysis:** Exclude UTI as mimicker
- **Type and screen:** If surgery likely
- **Water-soluble contrast study (Gastrografin):** Both diagnostic and therapeutic for adhesive SBO; contrast in colon at 4-8 hours predicts resolution without surgery (sensitivity 96%). Administer 100 mL Gastrografin via NG tube.

guidance.title: Bowel Obstruction
guidance.summary:
### Small Bowel Obstruction (SBO)
- **Cardinal symptoms:** Colicky abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting (often bilious), abdominal distension, obstipation (complete obstruction) or decreased flatus
- **Vomiting:** Early and prominent in proximal SBO; late in distal SBO
- **Distension:** Minimal in proximal SBO; prominent in distal SBO
- **Bowel sounds:** High-pitched, tinkling (early mechanical obstruction) or absent (late/ileus)
- **Pain pattern:** Intermittent cramping every 3-5 minutes (mechanical); constant pain suggests strangulation

**Common causes:** Adhesions from prior surgery (60-75%), incarcerated hernia (10-15%), malignancy, Crohn disease stricture, intussusception, gallstone ileus

### Large Bowel Obstruction (LBO)
- Progressive abdominal distension (dominant feature)
- Obstipation and failure to pass flatus
- Vomiting late (feculent)
- Pain is more constant and diffuse

**Common causes:** Colorectal carcinoma (60%), diverticular stricture, volvulus (sigmoid > cecal), fecal impaction

### Signs of Strangulation (Surgical Emergency)
- Constant (non-colicky) severe pain
- Fever, tachycardia
- Peritoneal signs (rebound, guarding, rigidity)
- Leukocytosis with left shift, elevated lactate
- Hemodynamic instability
- Bloody stool or NG aspirate
- CT findings: mesenteric edema, bowel wall thickening, pneumatosis, portal venous gas, reduced wall enhancement

### Closed-Loop Obstruction
- Single point of obstruction creates isolated segment — rapid ischemia
- Volvulus is the classic cause
- Competent ileocecal valve in LBO creates a closed loop (cecal diameter >12 cm = high perforation risk)

guidance.title: Intestinal Obstruction
guidance.summary:
An intestinal obstruction occurs when food or stool cannot move through the intestines. The obstruction can be complete or partial. There are many causes. The most common are adhesions , hernias , cancers, and certain medicines. 
 Symptoms include: 
 Severe abdominal pain or cramping 
 Vomiting 
 Bloating 
 Loud bowel sounds 
 Swelling of the abdomen 
 Inability to pass gas 
 Constipation 
 
 A complete intestinal obstruction is a medical emergency. It often requires surgery. 

 NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases

guidance.title: Back Pain — Emergency Evaluation
guidance.summary:
### Life-Threatening
- **Ruptured AAA** (`ruptured-aaa`): age > 60, sudden onset back/abdominal/flank pain, hypotension, pulsatile mass. Often misdiagnosed as renal colic. Classic triad (pain, hypotension, pulsatile mass) present in < 50%.
- **Aortic dissection** (`aortic-dissection`): tearing interscapular pain, hypertension, pulse deficits. Stanford B dissection presents primarily as back pain.
- **Spinal epidural abscess** (`spinal-epidural-abscess`): IVDU, immunosuppressed, or recent spinal procedure + fever + back pain → progressive neurological deficit. MRI with gadolinium is diagnostic. 4-phase progression: back pain → radiculopathy → motor deficit → paralysis. Time from onset to paralysis can be hours.
- **Cauda equina syndrome** (`cauda-equina-syndrome`): saddle anesthesia, urinary retention (most sensitive early finding), bilateral sciatica, decreased rectal tone. Surgical decompression within 48 hours of onset of urinary symptoms for best outcomes.
- **Spinal cord compression** (`spinal-cord-compression`): known malignancy + new back pain + neurological deficit. MRI entire spine (skip lesions in 10%). Dexamethasone 10 mg IV loading dose + emergent radiation oncology/neurosurgery.
- **Spinal cord injury** (`spinal-cord-injury`): trauma mechanism, midline tenderness, neurological deficit. Immobilize, CT then MRI.

### Emergent
- **Pyelonephritis** (`pyelonephritis`): flank pain, fever, CVA tenderness, pyuria, bacteriuria. Septic pyelonephritis requires IV antibiotics and admission.
- **Acute pancreatitis** (`acute-pancreatitis`): epigastric pain radiating to back, nausea/vomiting, lipase elevation

guidance.title: Acute Mesenteric Ischemia
guidance.summary:
### Classification

| Type | Frequency | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Arterial embolism (SMA) | 40-50% | Cardiac embolus (atrial fibrillation, valvular disease, recent MI, ventricular thrombus) |
| Arterial thrombosis (SMA) | 20-30% | Atherosclerotic stenosis with acute thrombosis; history of chronic mesenteric ischemia (postprandial pain, food fear, weight loss) |
| Mesenteric venous thrombosis (MVT) | 5-15% | Hypercoagulable state, portal hypertension, intra-abdominal inflammation, malignancy |
| Non-occlusive mesenteric ischemia (NOMI) | 5-15% | Low-flow state (cardiogenic shock, vasopressors, dialysis, cardiac surgery) |

### Key Clinical Features

- **Pain out of proportion to physical exam** — hallmark finding; severe periumbilical or diffuse abdominal pain with minimal tenderness early
- Rapid onset (minutes to hours) with arterial embolism; more insidious with MVT (days)
- Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea (often bloody in late stage)
- History of atrial fibrillation, recent cardiac catheterization, hypercoagulability, or atherosclerotic disease
- Peritoneal signs indicate bowel necrosis — this is a late and ominous finding
- Abdominal distension, absent bowel sounds in advanced disease

### High-Risk Populations
- Atrial fibrillation (especially without anticoagulation)
- Recent MI or cardiac surgery
- Peripheral vascular disease / known aortic atherosclerosis
- Hypercoagulable states (Factor V Leiden, malignancy, antiphospholipid syndrome)
- Chronic mesenteric ischemia (postprandial pain, weight loss) — at risk for acute thrombosis
- Heart failure patients on vasopressors or inotropes (NOMI)

1. **Diagnosing "ileus" without CT to exclude mechanical obstruction.** Post-operative ileus is a diagnosis of exclusion. A transition point on CT distinguishes mechanical SBO (requires surgical evaluation) from ileus (supportive care). CT changes management in 20-30% of cases initially thought to be ileus.

2. **Missing strangulation because labs are normal.** Lactate sensitivity for bowel ischemia is approximately 90% but specificity is low. Normal lactate does not exclude early strangulation. CT findings (reduced wall enhancement, mesenteric edema, pneumatosis) and clinical signs (constant pain, peritonitis, tachycardia) drive the decision.

3. **Delaying NG tube placement.** NG decompression reduces aspiration risk, relieves nausea, and allows quantification of losses for fluid replacement. Place early, not as a last resort.

4. **Under-resuscitating.** Third-space losses in bowel obstruction are massive (3-6 L). Patients presenting with tachycardia and oliguria need aggressive crystalloid before any decision about operative vs. non-operative management.

5. **Failing to examine all hernia orifices.** Incarcerated inguinal, femoral, umbilical, and incisional hernias cause SBO. Missed femoral hernias in elderly women are a classic and preventable diagnostic failure. Examine the groin in every patient with SBO.

6. **Prolonging non-operative management beyond 72 hours for complete SBO.** The risk of strangulation increases with duration. If Gastrografin has not reached the colon by 8 hours, or there is no clinical improvement by 72 hours, surgery is indicated.

1. **Relying solely on initial CT to exclude bowel injury.** CT sensitivity is only 60-95% for hollow viscus injury. Free fluid without solid organ injury on CT should raise suspicion. Serial exams and repeat imaging at 6-12 hours are essential.

2. **Discharging a patient with seatbelt sign after a "negative" CT.** Seatbelt sign carries 3-8x risk of bowel injury. These patients require 24-hour observation with serial abdominal exams regardless of initial CT findings.

|---|---|
| **Biliary colic** | Episodic, colicky RUQ pain lasting < 6 hours; resolves spontaneously; no fever, no leukocytosis, no gallbladder wall thickening; negative Murphy sign |
| **Ascending cholangitis** | Charcot triad (fever, jaundice, RUQ pain); Reynolds pentad adds hypotension and altered mental status; CBD dilation on ultrasound; conjugated hyperbilirubinemia and elevated ALP/GGT prominent; jaundice more common than in cholecystitis |
| **Acute pancreatitis** | Epigastric pain radiating to back; lipase > 3x upper limit of normal; may coexist with cholecystitis (gallstone pancreatitis) |
| **Peptic ulcer disease / perforation** | Epigastric pain; free air on upright CXR or CT if perforated; no gallbladder wall thickening |
| **Acute hepatitis** | Transaminases > 1,000 IU/L (much higher than cholecystitis); hepatomegaly; risk factors (viral exposure, alcohol, medications) |
| **Acute appendicitis (high-riding cecum)** | RLQ pain typical, but can present as RUQ pain with retrocecal or subhepatic appendix; CT distinguishes |
| **Right lower lobe pneumonia** | Referred RUQ pain from diaphragmatic irritation; cough, pleuritic component; CXR abnormal |
| **Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome** | Perihepatitis from PID; young women; RUQ pain with elevated ESR; cervical motion tenderness on pelvic exam |
| **Renal colic (right)** | Flank pain radiating to groin; hematuria; no gallbladder findings on ultrasound; CT KUB shows ureteral stone |
